amb.1: The wheels knock out their old rhythm: ta-tam, ta-tam, ta-tam.
amb.2: A glass rattles in its holder somewhere, and then goes still.
amb.3: Far ahead, the locomotive calls into the dark, long and low.
amb.4: A moth beats against the corridor lamp, again and again.
amb.5: The smell of coal smoke and wormwood seeps in through the window frames.
amb.6: A level-crossing bell rings past and fades behind you.
amb.7: Someone coughs behind a door, then turns over with a creak of springs.
amb.8: The samovar ticks as it cools, like a clock no one wound.

n.arrival:
06:00. The brakes sigh, long and weary. Qumtepa. A low station of yellow brick, a water tower, a dusty acacia, and beyond them the desert, pink in the first light, stretching away as flat and quiet as a sheet on a line.

The passengers gather their things, yawning, counting their bags. The night is over, whether you are ready for it or not.
n.arrival.safe:
06:00. The brakes sigh, long and weary. Qumtepa. A low station of yellow brick, a water tower, the desert pink in the first light. Somewhere in your carriage, a geologist is putting on his shoes for the first time since half past ten last night.

On the platform, a militia captain waits with his hands behind his back, as he does for every train. Rudin is already at the door with his folder, first in line to leave.
n.arrival.taken:
06:00. The brakes sigh: Qumtepa. A low station of yellow brick, a water tower, and the desert pink in the first light. The professor is somewhere far behind you in the dark, and the folded tracing paper presses against your ribs with every breath.

Passengers step down, yawning, stretching. Nobody on this platform knows what happened at Saksovul. Not yet.
n.baggage:
The padlock opens with a clack. Inside, the baggage car is a dark cave of crates, mail sacks and melons that smell of summer. You raise your lamp.

"Close the door," says a calm voice. "There is a draught, and I am old."

Professor Arslan Nuriev sits on a crate between two sacks of post, in his socks, his shoes neatly placed beside him, a stub of candle in a tin. He looks at you over his spectacles as if you were a promising but late student. "Ah. The conductor. Either you are cleverer than I hoped, or I was more careless than I thought."
n.baggage.again: The baggage car: crates, mail sacks, the sweet smell of melons, the candle stub burning low in its tin. The professor sits on his crate with his shoes still neatly paired beside him, a rock sample turning in his fingers like a worry bead. He raises a hand in greeting, as calm as a man in his own study. "News from the outside world, conductor?"
n.c2:
Compartment 2. Valentin Rudin sits by the window with his folder on his knees, as neat as a closed drawer. A cigarette burns in a holder; the air smells of cloves. He looks up at you the way a clerk looks at a form that has been filled in wrongly.

"Conductor. Have they found our professor? No? A pity. Some people simply prefer to vanish."
n.c2.dawn: Compartment 2. Rudin has not slept. He sits with his coat on, the folder clamped under his arm, and stares out at the brightening steppe as if it owes him money. He does not look at you. The ashtray is full of half-smoked cigarettes, every one stubbed out in anger.
n.c2.empty:
Compartment 2 is empty. Rudin has gone to the dining car — the chef said he dines at half past eleven, regular as a clock. His grey coat hangs on the hook. The leather folder is not on the table; something flat makes a neat bump under his pillow.

The corridor behind you is quiet. For now.
n.c2.gone: Compartment 2 is empty and stripped. Rudin got off at Saksovul with his men and his prize. Only the smell of cloves remains, and a single burnt match on the table, laid exactly parallel to the edge.
n.c2_search:
Your hands are cold and steady. Under the pillow lies the leather folder. Inside: blank forms with a ministry header, a list of land plots around Qumtepa with prices pencilled beside them — absurdly small prices — and a telegram form, received at Oltinsoy this afternoon.

TO V RUDIN TRAIN 17 CAR 7 STOP SAKSOVUL 0400 THREE MEN AND CAR READY STOP BRING GEOLOGIST WITH PAPERS STOP NO FUSS STOP K

Somewhere in the dining car, a spoon rings against a glass. You do not have long.
n.c4: Compartment 4. Lola sits on the lower berth with her knees drawn up, the anatomy textbook open and unread on her lap. The professor's coat still hangs on its hook; she has not touched it. The window has been closed. "Any news?" she asks, and then, seeing your face: "No. Of course not."
n.c4.late: Compartment 4. Lola sits with her knees drawn up, the textbook unread on her lap. The briefcase is gone — it vanished when the lights failed, and nobody has seen it since. Only the professor's coat remains, swaying on its hook with the rhythm of the wheels.
n.c4.reunited: Compartment 4 is empty but warm. Lola's textbook lies closed on the berth with the photograph on top of it, face up — a girl on her father's shoulders, mountains behind them. For the first time tonight, nobody is hiding it.
n.c4.taken: Compartment 4. Lola has not cried; she sits very straight, staring at the professor's empty coat. "They had papers," she says. "Everyone always has papers." She does not look at you, and you cannot blame her.
n.c5:
Compartment 5 smells of cheap cologne and shoe polish. Gena Sorokin has spread his sample cases across both berths: gleaming 'Swallow' sewing machines, bobbins, catalogues. He greets you like a long-lost cousin. "Conductor! Sit, sit. You look like a person who needs a sewing machine and doesn't know it yet."

His wallet lies on the table, unusually fat for a man who sighs about debts.
n.c5.ally: Compartment 5. Gena has packed his samples away and sits on the edge of the berth with his jacket on, like a man waiting for a fight he has decided to show up for. He winks at you. "Saksovul, brother. I'll be on the platform. Loud as a brass band."
n.c6:
Compartment 6 smells of dried apricots and valerian drops. Halima-buvi sits wrapped in a shawl, wide awake despite her heart drops, and Malika the hen sits on her basket in the corner like a black queen on a throne, sitting oddly high — as if the straw beneath her were stuffed with something.

"Come in, come in, child. Old women don't sleep on trains. We watch."
n.c6.hiding: Compartment 6. Halima-buvi has hung a shawl across the upper berth like a curtain. Behind it, very quietly, someone is breathing. Malika sits on her basket at the foot of the berth like a sentry. "Nobody comes in here without asking me first," the old woman says. "And I don't hear well tonight."
n.corridor: The corridor of carriage 7, {time}. Lamps swing in their brackets; glasses chime softly in the samovar rack. Behind the doors, the passengers are only pretending to sleep. Through the window, the steppe runs past in the dark, black on black.
n.corridor.dawn_safe: The corridor of carriage 7, {time}. Saksovul is behind you. The sky in the east has turned the colour of weak tea, and the first larks are rising over the steppe. The professor is safe — for now. There is still time to make this night mean something before Qumtepa.
n.corridor.dawn_taken: The corridor of carriage 7, {time}. Saksovul is behind you, and so is the professor. Grey light creeps along the carpet. The folded tracing paper in your tunic crackles each time you breathe, as if to remind you it is there.
n.corridor.first:
The corridor of carriage 7 sways under your feet: brass rails, a strip of red carpet, the samovar ticking at the far end. Doors to compartments 2, 4, 5 and 6; your staff room by the samovar; the front vestibule leads to the dining car, the rear vestibule to the coal bin and the locked baggage car.

It is {time}. The professor is somewhere on this train — or he is not. Every minute you spend looking is a minute you are not pouring tea or punching tickets, and the chief notices everything. At four, the train stops at Saksovul. At six, Qumtepa.
n.corridor.night: The corridor of carriage 7, {time}. Deep night. The lamps have been turned down to a yellow glow, and the carriage rocks like a cradle. Someone snores in compartment 5; someone does not sleep at all in compartment 2. Out in the dark, the steppe has no beginning and no end.
n.d_chief_report:
Matvey listens with his cap pushed back, his face slowly turning the colour of a beetroot. "Missing? Nobody goes missing on my train." He makes a note in his book, underlines it twice. "Search the carriage. Quietly. If he hasn't turned up by Saksovul, we'll hand it to the station there."

You both speak louder than you should. When you step back into the corridor, the door of compartment 2 is open a crack, and a thread of clove-scented smoke drifts out of it. It closes as you pass.
n.d_comp4:
Compartment 4 is cold. The window has been lowered, and the steppe night pours in with the smell of wormwood and engine smoke. The professor's coat hangs on its hook. His shoes are gone. His briefcase lies on the lower berth, its clasps undone, as if someone wanted it to be found.

Lola stands in the doorway hugging herself. Down the corridor, the carriage sleeps — or pretends to.

You are a conductor, not a detective. But the professor was your passenger, and the night is long.
n.d_knock:
22:40. You have barely sat down with your ledger when someone knocks — no, hammers — at the staff-room door.

It is Lola, without her shoes, her face the colour of the tablecloth. "He's gone," she says. "I went to wash my face, I was gone five minutes, ten at most, and when I came back — he's gone. The window is open. His briefcase is still there. His coat is still there." She grips your sleeve. "People don't just fall out of trains. Do they?"

Behind her, at the far end of the corridor, the door of compartment 2 closes with a quiet click.
n.dining: The dining car glows like a lantern. Bahodir the chef — a mountain in a white jacket with a cap balanced on top — polishes glasses behind the counter while coffee seethes in a copper pot. Crates of melons are stacked by the door. "Ah, the conductor of carriage 7! You look like a person who has a problem and no coffee. One of these I can fix."
n.dining.closed: The dining car is dark, the chairs upturned on the tables like dead beetles. A snore rumbles from the pantry behind the counter: Bahodir sleeps among his melons. The dining car closed at one o'clock, and Bahodir does not open it again for anyone.
n.dining.rudin: The dining car glows like a lantern. Bahodir polishes glasses behind the counter. At the corner table, Valentin Rudin eats his supper with small precise movements, cutting the meat into squares of equal size. He does not look up at you. He does not need to.
n.duty_tea:
You carry the tea round on a tray, glasses chiming in their holders. Passengers talk while you pour; they always do.

Halima-buvi takes two lumps of sugar and asks after "the tall one in socks". Gena tells you a joke about a sewing machine and a camel that nearly makes you spill. Lola holds her glass without drinking. In compartment 2, Rudin watches you pour and says, almost gently: "A man who climbs out of a train window usually does not wish to be found, conductor. Better to let him go. For everyone."

The chief will be pleased. Nobody can say carriage 7 went thirsty.
n.duty_tickets:
You go from door to door with your punch. Halima-buvi's ticket is wrapped in a handkerchief. Lola's is in her textbook. Gena's ticket, you notice, was bought this afternoon at the same window as the grey man's — the numbers run one after the other, as if they queued together.

Rudin hands you his ticket without looking up. Oltinsoy–Qumtepa, compartment 2. One corner is missing, torn off in a little triangle.
n.e1_daybreak:
You step in front of Rudin as he reaches the exit. "Captain Usmonov! A word, please."

You lay it out on the bench beneath the water tower, piece by piece: the evidence you have gathered through the night. It is not everything, but it is enough, and every piece points the same way — to Saksovul, to three men and a car, to the man in grey. Rudin begins to say something about the ministry. Then the professor steps down from carriage 7 with his daughter's arm through his, and says, quite calmly, "I will testify. All of it."

The captain looks at the old man, at the young woman, at you. Then he puts a hand on Rudin's shoulder. "Comrade. Let us talk in my office."

By noon the whole station knows. By evening, so does the newspaper. In the spring, the first well is drilled into the Qumtepa sand, and the water that comes up is sweet. Lola writes to you twice a year. Her father signs the letters too.
n.e2_quiet:
You stop Rudin by the water tower and tell Captain Usmonov everything you know. It is a long story. It sounds, even to you, like a story.

The captain listens politely. He looks at what you hold out to him; it is not enough. A man in a grey coat with ministry papers on one side, and on the other a conductor's word and a geologist who will not say whom he was hiding from. "I can't arrest a ministry man for being unpleasant on a train," Usmonov says at last. Rudin raises his hat to you both and walks away into the morning crowd, unhurried.

The professor shakes your hand for a long time. "You saved an old man's skin," he says. "That is not nothing." It is not nothing. But you know Rudin's kind: he will be back, with better papers, and next time there may be no conductor on duty who cares.
n.e3_deal:
The envelope is thick and smells of cloves. You tell him where to look. You do not watch them take the professor; you are busy with your samovar, just as you promised.

At Qumtepa you count the money in the staff room with the curtain drawn. One hundred roubles: more than two months' wages. You buy a good coat with it, and a radio, and it all wears out faster than it should.

That winter the newspapers report that a private consortium has bought up most of the desert around Qumtepa "at prices reflecting its total unsuitability for agriculture". In the spring, a little later, they report the discovery of a vast fresh-water reservoir beneath the very same sand. The price of water in Qumtepa triples. Then triples again.

You never find out what happened to the professor. Sometimes, pouring tea on the night train, you catch the smell of cloves, and your hands are not quite steady.
n.e4_wrong:
Captain Usmonov has been waiting all night for someone to hand him a culprit, and you have just handed him one. He nods slowly, signals to his men, and the person you pointed at is led away across the platform, turning to look back at you with an expression you will remember for the rest of your life.

It does not take long for the case to fall apart. A few days, a few questions, a few telephone calls. By then the person is released, and the shame has stuck to them like coal dust, and the professor — if anyone is still looking for him — has gone wherever such people go.

Rudin, of course, walked off the platform while everyone was busy. He even raised his hat to you as he passed. You did not notice at the time. You only remember it later, at night, when you cannot sleep.
n.e5_junction:
The car beyond Saksovul station drives off into the dark with its lights out, and with it goes the professor, his shoes neatly tied, his secret somewhere in his head where no paper can reach it.

At Qumtepa, Captain Usmonov writes down what you tell him and files it under "passenger left the train at Saksovul of his own free will, accompanied by colleagues". The stamp on the men's paper was perfectly genuine. That is the worst of it: everything was genuine.

You go on working the night train. Every time it stops at Saksovul for its twenty minutes, you look out at the lonely lamp on the platform and the dark beyond the station building, and you count the minutes until the whistle. Years later you read a short notice in a newspaper about a geologist, retired, who lives quietly in a small town and does not give interviews. You hope it is him. You will never know.
n.e6_rails:
You fight. You are a conductor, not a soldier, and Rudin is stronger than his cuffs suggest. There is a moment of air, the roar of the wheels very close, a long fall through the dark — and then nothing.

You wake at dawn in the dry grass beside the embankment, with a split lip, a twisted ankle and the whole sky over you, pale and enormous. The rails hum faintly and then fall silent. Somewhere far away, the "Southern Star" is pulling into Qumtepa without you.

A shepherd finds you at noon and takes you to the next village on his donkey. By the time you get back to the railway, there is a report about a conductor who "left the train in an intoxicated state", signed by a witness from the ministry. Nobody asks you about a professor. Nobody wants to know.
n.e7_relieved:
"Enough." Chief Conductor Matvey takes your cap off your head with his own hands. "Twenty-two years I've run this line, and I have never seen a carriage in such a state. Cold samovar, tickets unpunched, the conductor wandering about like a lost goat."

He locks you in the staff room — for your own good, he says — and takes the carriage himself. Through the door you hear the night go on without you: voices, footsteps, doors sliding, the train stopping at Saksovul, men's voices, the train moving again. You hammer on the door once. Nobody comes.

At Qumtepa, Matvey lets you out and hands you a form to sign. Whatever happened to the professor happened while you sat on your bunk staring at the chief's orders above the samovar. You will read about it, if you ever do, in someone else's newspaper.
n.e8_keeper:
You walk past the captain, past Rudin's grey back, straight to the young woman with the notebook. "Dilnoza Rahimova? This belongs to Professor Nuriev. It belongs to everyone, really." You put the folded tracing paper into her hands, a black feather still caught in the fold.

She opens it, reads the stamp, the depths, the word LENS, and her face changes. The photographer starts taking pictures of the map, of you, of the train, of everything.

Three days later the Qumtepa Truth runs it on the front page: A SEA UNDER THE SAND. The story is picked up in the capital within a week. Once the whole republic knows what lies beneath the desert, nobody can buy it for the price of a dune; the land sales are frozen, the survey is published, and a certain ministry man is quietly transferred somewhere very cold.

In December a letter comes from Nuriev, in a draughtsman's hand: "You gave away my map. Thank you." Inside is a black feather.
n.ev_chief_round:
Chief Conductor Matvey comes through the carriage on his eleven o'clock round, lamp in hand, checking the ashtrays, the samovar and you, in that order. He smells of machine oil and strong tobacco, and he walks the corridor the way other men walk their own garden. "Well? Anything I should know about carriage 7?"

Behind him, the door of compartment 2 stands open a hand's width. Nobody inside is reading.
n.ev_chief_round.informed: Chief Conductor Matvey comes through on his eleven o'clock round, lamp in hand, checking the ashtrays, the samovar and you, in that order. "Well? Has our geologist turned up? No?" He chews his moustache. "The ministry man has asked me twice now about the baggage car. Twice. I don't like being asked things twice on my own train." He waits, as if you might have an answer to that.
n.ev_gena_cards: Gena Sorokin catches your sleeve in the corridor, all teeth and cologne. "Conductor! Brother! Just one round. A man can't sell sewing machines all night — he needs a little human company." He fans a deck of cards under your nose with a magician's flourish. Inside his jacket, as it falls open, you glimpse a fat envelope. "Forty minutes, no more. I'll even let you win. Word of a salesman."
n.ev_hen_restless: Someone tugs your sleeve: Halima-buvi, in her shawl, a candle in a saucer. "Child, Malika won't settle. She keeps pecking at her straw as if there's a snake in it. An old woman's hands are not what they were." She looks at you very directly. "Will you come and look? I'd rather it was you than anyone else on this train."
n.ev_inspection: 05:00. Chief Conductor Matvey makes his final inspection, slower than usual, as if the night has aged him too. He runs a finger along the brass rail and inspects it for dust. He counts the glasses in the rack. He opens the samovar tap, looks into your ledger, and then, at last, into your face, as if that were one more thing on his list to check before Qumtepa.
n.ev_junction:
04:00. Saksovul. The brakes scream, the carriage shudders and stops beside a platform lit by a single lamp. Beyond the station building an engine idles: a car with its headlights off.

Three men in rain capes climb into carriage 7 as if they own it. Rudin meets them at the door. One of them shows Matvey a paper with a stamp; Matvey reads it twice, his face like a closed fist. "Twenty minutes," Rudin says pleasantly. "We are looking for a sick passenger. We have come to take him home."

They start towards the back of the train.
n.ev_lights:
Half past one. The lamps flicker, sigh, and go out. The whole carriage plunges into blackness so complete you can hear it: the wheels louder, someone gasping, Malika the hen shrieking in compartment 6.

In the dark, a door slides open — not far from you. Footsteps, soft and quick, heading towards compartment 4.

The electrician will need fifteen minutes. You have fewer.
n.ev_rudin_attack:
The vestibule light is out. The outer door is open — you feel the wind before you see it, the steppe roaring past a metre from your boots. And Rudin is there, his coat off, his sleeves rolled up like a man about to do some honest work.

"You have become inconvenient," he says almost sadly. "Trains are dangerous at night. Conductors fall from them every year. Nobody writes to the newspapers."
n.ev_rudin_chat:
Rudin is waiting for you in the front vestibule, smoking, as if by chance. He offers you a cigarette from a silver case. "You work hard, conductor. Too hard. A professor wanders off, and suddenly you are everywhere — compartments, vestibules, the baggage car. People notice."

He smiles, and the smile does not reach anywhere. "I am a reasonable man. Reasonable men reward other reasonable men." A folded banknote appears between two of his fingers, as if he had grown it there.
n.ev_rudin_threat:
The vestibule door slams behind you, and Rudin is there, very close, the clove smell suffocating. He does not raise his voice. He never does.

"Let us stop pretending. You know where he is, or you will soon. At Saksovul some colleagues of mine will board. You will look the other way. You will be busy with your samovar. And afterwards you will have a long, quiet, comfortable career." He straightens your collar with two fingers. "Or a short one."
n.ev_tea_late:
Half past eleven, and the samovar in carriage 7 has not been touched. Chief Conductor Matvey finds a queue of thirsty passengers in the corridor and Halima-buvi holding an empty glass like an accusation.

"Twenty-two years I've run this line," Matvey says very quietly, which is worse than shouting, "and nobody has ever gone without tea in my train." He writes something in his book.
n.ev_tickets_late: Half past twelve. Matvey stands in your staff-room doorway with the ticket ledger open, every column empty. "An inspector boards at Saksovul sometimes," he says, very quietly. "If he finds a whole carriage of unpunched tickets, it is my name in his report. Mine. Twenty-two years without a single remark." He writes something in his book, pressing so hard that the pencil tears the page.
n.gena_confront:
You remind him of the card table: the brand-new fifty-rouble notes, the envelope with a ministry frank, the way he kept glancing towards compartment 2. Gena's grin slides off his face like butter off a hot knife.

"All right. All right." He lowers his voice. "The man in grey. At the Oltinsoy buffet, before we boarded. Fifty roubles to keep the conductor busy tonight — cards, complaints, a burst pipe, anything. That's all, I swear on my mother. I didn't know there'd be a professor. I didn't know anything." He shows you the envelope: "For the distraction — V.R." in a small, precise hand.
n.halima_basket:
Halima-buvi looks at you for a long time. Then she lifts Malika off the basket — the hen protests like a whole kolkhoz — and pushes aside the straw.

Underneath lies a sheet of tracing paper, folded in four, a black feather caught in the fold. You open it. A survey map of the Qumtepa desert: contour lines drawn with a draughtsman's hand, borehole numbers, depths, and in the middle a vast blue shape marked LENS — FRESH WATER — EST. VOLUME… The expedition stamp is in every corner.

"He put it there while I slept," the old woman says. "I wasn't sleeping. Some secrets are safer under a hen than in a safe. Now it's yours to keep, child. Keep it well."
n.j_followed:
The baggage car is empty. For one moment Rudin looks almost foolish — and then he turns, without hurry, and looks straight at you. He has been watching you all night, and he has been counting doors.

"Shall we stop wasting time?" he says, and walks back down the corridor towards the hiding place, the three rain capes behind him. You get there first. Barely.
n.j_safe:
They search the baggage car crate by crate, sack by sack, slitting a melon in their fury. Nothing. They search the vestibule, the coal bin, the gangway. Nothing. The locomotive whistles; Matvey looks at his watch and says, to nobody in particular, "Twenty minutes."

The three rain capes climb down onto the platform. The car beyond the station drives away into the dark. Rudin stays aboard: he has a ticket to Qumtepa, after all. He passes you in the corridor without a word, white around the mouth.

The train jerks, and Saksovul slides away behind you.
n.j_safe.allies:
You stand in the doorway, and it turns out you are not alone. Doors bang open along the corridor. Someone you stood by tonight now stands by you: there is shouting about railway papers and rights and witnesses, there are sleepy faces at every door, and the rain capes, who came for one quiet sick passenger, find themselves in the middle of a public scene.

They look at one another. Somebody is going to remember their faces. The locomotive whistles; they climb down. The car beyond the station drives away into the dark, and Rudin stays aboard, white around the mouth.
n.j_safe.chief:
You plant yourself in front of the baggage car door. When the rain capes reach you, Matvey is suddenly at your shoulder, all twenty-two years of him. "This car is railway property," he says. "I've read your paper. It says nothing about my baggage car. Bring me a paper from the railway, signed and stamped, and I'll open it myself."

They argue. Matvey does not move; he has the gift of a man who has never once been late into Qumtepa. The locomotive whistles. The rain capes climb down, the car beyond the station drives away, and Rudin stays aboard, white around the mouth. Saksovul slides away behind you.
n.j_safe.gena:
You catch Gena's eye and nod. A moment later the platform explodes: Gena Sorokin, in his vest, is shouting that someone has stolen his sample case, that he knows his rights, that he will write to Moscow, to the newspapers, to his mother. The station militiaman comes running; the rain capes, who do not wish to be remembered by militiamen, hesitate on the steps.

Twenty minutes are not very long. The locomotive whistles. The car beyond the station drives away, empty. Rudin stays aboard, white around the mouth, and Gena climbs back in at the last second, grinning like a wedding drummer.
n.j_taken:
It takes them less than five minutes. The professor does not struggle; he puts on his shoes, ties the laces neatly, and walks between the rain capes as if to a lecture. On the platform he turns and lifts one hand to you — not a reproach, not a farewell, just a small, tired salute.

Rudin is the last to step down. He touches his hat. The car beyond the station starts its engine, and its red lights shrink into the steppe until there is nothing left but the dark.
n.j_taken.lola:
It takes them less than five minutes. Lola throws herself at the rain capes and is pushed aside like a curtain. The professor puts on his shoes, ties the laces neatly, and kisses his daughter on the forehead. "Fifteen years too late, and five minutes too short," he says. "Still. Better than nothing."

Rudin touches his hat to you as he steps down. The car beyond the station drives away, its red lights shrinking into the steppe, and Lola stands on the platform until the guard drags her back aboard.
n.p_chief:
Chief Conductor Matvey fills the doorway of your staff room like a wardrobe in uniform. He has run this line for twenty-two years and has never once been late into Qumtepa.

"Rules for tonight," he says, counting on thick fingers. "Tea round by half past eleven. Tickets checked by half past twelve. Coal in the samovar — I want it hot at my five o'clock inspection. Saksovul junction at four, twenty minutes' stop, nobody wanders." He lowers his voice. "And a man from the ministry rides in your carriage. Whatever he wants, he gets. I'll be round at eleven."
n.p_departure:
Oltinsoy, 22:00. The river breathes cold mist across the platform, and train No. 17, the "Southern Star", hisses like a samovar about to boil. You stand at the door of carriage 7 with your lamp and your punch, cap straight, collar buttoned, the way Chief Conductor Matvey likes it.

Your passengers come out of the mist one by one. An old woman with a wicker basket that clucks. A young woman dragging a suitcase heavier than she is, who keeps glancing at the lit windows. A man in a grey coat with a thin leather folder, followed by a loud fellow juggling two sample cases. Last, a tall grey-bearded man who holds his briefcase against his chest like a child.

The whistle blows. You have one pair of hands.
n.p_halima:
"Careful, child, careful — Malika does not like to fly." The basket is surprisingly heavy. Under a cloth, a black hen regards you with one furious orange eye.

The old woman introduces herself as Halima-buvi, compartment 6, going to Qumtepa for her granddaughter's wedding. She presses a dried apricot into your palm as payment. "I take my heart drops at eleven and then I sleep like a stone," she says. "Malika keeps watch. Nobody touches my basket while Malika is on it."

As you settle her, the tall bearded man passes in the corridor. Halima-buvi follows him with her eyes. "That one walks like a man who has lost his sleep somewhere and is looking for it."
n.p_lola:
The suitcase is full of books — you can hear them shift like bricks. The young woman thanks you twice, then a third time, as if she has forgotten she already did. Lola Karimova, medical student, compartment 4.

At the door of the compartment she stops. Inside, the tall bearded man is arranging his things. Lola does not go in. "Is he… is that man travelling all the way to Qumtepa?" she asks quietly. "Please don't tell him I asked."

A corner of a photograph sticks out of her anatomy textbook. She pushes it back in with one finger and steps inside, looking at the floor.
n.p_professor:
You carry a glass of tea to compartment 4. The bearded man takes it in both hands and nods. "Arslan Nuriev. Geologist. A boring man with boring rocks," he says, as if he has rehearsed it.

Lola is pretending to read on the upper berth. Neither of them looks at the other; the silence between them is so thick you could slice it.

The professor turns the glass in its holder. "Tell me — the baggage car at the end. Is it locked at night? Who keeps the key?" You tell him: the chief has one, and Bahodir the chef keeps a spare for his crates. "And how long do we stand at Saksovul?" Twenty minutes. He nods slowly, as though adding up a column of figures.
n.p_rudin:
The man in grey hands you his ticket without looking at you. "Valentin Rudin. Ministry." When you ask which ministry, he smiles with half of his mouth. "The kind that need not concern a conductor." He smells of cloves and expensive tobacco. Compartment 2.

His companion is not his companion at all — he only walked in his shadow. "Gena Sorokin, sewing machines, the 'Swallow' model, finest stitch in the republic!" Compartment 5. He tries to sell you a machine before you have punched his ticket.

As you turn to go, Rudin speaks again, softly. "The professor in compartment 4. Does he sleep soundly, would you say?"
n.platform:
The platform smells of dust and locomotive steam. Captain Usmonov of the station militia stands by the water tower with his hands behind his back, watching the passengers pass like a farmer counting sheep. Porters shout; a woman sells hot samsa from a basket. Rudin walks briskly towards the exit, folder under his arm, without looking back.

This is the last moment when anything you say will matter.
n.platform.reporter:
The platform smells of dust and locomotive steam. Captain Usmonov of the station militia stands by the water tower, watching the passengers pass. Rudin walks briskly towards the exit, folder under his arm.

And by the timetable board, exactly as the telegram promised, a young woman with a notebook and a photographer with a heavy camera are searching the crowd for a grey-bearded geologist: Dilnoza Rahimova of the Qumtepa Truth.

This is the last moment when anything you say will matter.
n.prof_talk:
"At half past ten I came back from the washroom and found a man in grey with both hands in my briefcase. Wrong compartment, he said." The professor smiles without humour. "So I drew him a beautiful map of nothing, with a well in the middle of the salt flats. I opened the window a crack, pushed the latch with a pencil, and hid the real map where nobody would look: under a hen that has not laid since summer.

"Under the Qumtepa desert there is fresh water — a sea under the sand, enough for a hundred years. Whoever buys that land cheap before the survey is published will own the water. Your man in grey has friends waiting at Saksovul.

"Testify? Against a ministry? For myself, no. I had a daughter once. She would be about your age. For her, perhaps, I would stand up in front of anyone."
n.rear: The rear vestibule is cold and roaring; the floor plates shift under your boots. The coal bin stands against the wall with its scuttle and shovel, and the samovar flue runs up beside it. Beyond the rattling gangway is the door of the baggage car: iron, painted green, padlocked. Above the gangway, a ventilation hatch the size of a schoolbag.
n.reunion:
You walk her through the swaying train. She stops twice. The second time she nearly turns back.

The professor stands up when he sees her, too fast, and knocks over the candle. For a moment neither of them speaks. Then Lola holds out the photograph, and the professor takes it in both hands the way he took the glass of tea — carefully, as if it might burn.

"You've grown," he says, which is the stupidest and truest thing anyone has said all night. Lola laughs and cries at the same time. You find you have urgent business elsewhere.
n.sherzod:
You set Bahodir's bread and cheese on the coal bin and wait. Then a pair of thin legs appear in the ventilation hatch, and a boy drops onto the gangway — eleven at most, in a man's padded jacket with the sleeves rolled four times.

He eats first and talks second. Sherzod, from a kolkhoz near Oltinsoy, going to his uncle in Qumtepa, ticket-less and proud of it. He lives among the melons. "At half past ten I saw the grey man come out of compartment 4 backwards, smiling. Then the tall man with the beard came, in his socks, shoes in his hand, and slipped into the baggage car when the cook left the door open. He saw me. He put a finger on his lips and gave me a sweet. He said, 'Let them chase the window.'"
n.staff: Your staff room: a narrow bunk, a tiny table bolted to the wall, the ledger, the key board, the chief's orders pinned above the samovar valve. It is the only place on the train that is yours, and tonight it feels like a cupboard someone is about to open.
n.staff.hiding: Your staff room. The professor sits folded onto your bunk behind the drawn curtain, his knees nearly touching his beard, holding a glass of your tea. It is the first place anyone would look — and you both know it. "Don't worry about me," he whispers. "Worry about the man who is worried about me."
note.bahodir_talked: Bahodir: the baggage car door "felt heavier" after 22:35. A reporter, D. Rahimova, will meet the professor on the Qumtepa platform at 06:00. Rudin dines 23:30–00:45.
note.chief_informed: The chief knows the professor is missing. Rudin overheard.
note.gena_ally: Gena will stand with you at Saksovul.
note.gena_cards: Gena paid at cards with brand-new notes from an envelope with a ministry frank.
note.gena_talked: Gena has debts, but also a fat wallet and "a generous friend".
note.halima_talked: Halima-buvi saw the professor walk to the back of the train in his socks. Malika sits "heavy, like on eggs".
note.hid_halima: The professor is hidden behind Halima-buvi's shawl in compartment 6.
note.hid_staff: The professor is hidden in your staff room.
note.lola_talked: Lola hides a photograph in her textbook and won't talk about it yet.
note.map_returned: You gave the real map back to the professor.
note.met_rudin: Rudin asked whether the professor sleeps soundly — before anything had happened.
note.note_baggage: The professor asked who keeps the baggage car key, and how long the stop at Saksovul is.
note.note_ministry: The chief was ordered by telegram to "assist Comrade Rudin in every way".
note.prof_knows_lola: The professor knows Lola is on the train.
note.prof_taken: The professor was taken off at Saksovul. You still have the map.
note.prof_told: The professor faked his escape. Under the desert lies a sea of fresh water. He won't testify for himself — only, perhaps, for a daughter.
note.promised_rudin: You promised Rudin to look the other way at Saksovul.
note.read_orders: The chief's orders say Rudin will alight at Saksovul "with a travelling companion".
note.reunited: Lola and her father have found each other.
note.rudin_talked: Rudin keeps asking about luggage and the baggage car.
note.rudin_water: Rudin: "Water belongs to whoever can afford the pipes."
note.saw_searcher: In the blackout, a man smelling of cloves grabbed the briefcase from compartment 4.
note.sherzod_heard: A child is hiding in the baggage car and wants bread.
note.took_bribe: You took twenty roubles from Rudin.
r.ally: Gena looks at you for a long moment, then at the envelope, then at you again. "You know what, brother? I sell sewing machines. I don't sell people." He puts out his hand. "At Saksovul, I'm yours. Whatever you need — a scandal, a fistfight, a song."
r.ally_no: Gena shakes his head, sweating. "Brother, I barely know you. That man has friends with cars. You want me to stick my neck out for a conductor I met tonight?" He does not say no forever. But he needs to trust you more than this.
r.baggage.give_map: He unfolds the tracing paper, checks the stamps, the depths, the blue lens in the middle, and lets out a breath he seems to have held since Oltinsoy. "Under a hen," he murmurs. "Science owes that bird a debt." He folds it into his inner pocket. "Thank you. You did not have to."
r.baggage.hide_halima: Halima-buvi opens the door before you knock, as if she has been waiting. She hangs a shawl across the upper berth like a curtain and pushes the professor behind it. "In my village we hid a whole wedding from the tax inspector," she says. "One professor is nothing." Malika settles on her basket by the door, on guard.
r.baggage.hide_staff: You wait for a long straight stretch, when the corridor is empty, and walk him through the carriage in his socks to your staff room, the curtain drawn across your bunk. It is warm there, and close. It is also the first place anyone would look.
r.baggage.leave: "Lock it," he agrees. "And keep the key in your pocket, not on a hook. Hooks are for coats and fools." The padlock clacks shut behind you.
r.baggage.tell_lola:
You tell him about the photograph. Chimgan, 1961. A little girl on a bearded man's shoulders.

The professor does not move for a long time. The candle flame leans with the train. "Lola," he says at last, as if testing whether the word still works. "Lola is on this train. In my compartment. And I climbed out of the window to get away from — " He takes off his spectacles and presses his fingers to his eyes. "Bring her. Please. If she will come."
r.briefcase:
Folders of rock samples, a pencil case, a map of the Qumtepa desert. You spread the map on the berth — and frown. The ink is still fresh enough to smudge under your thumb. The legend is careless, the contour lines drawn freehand, and the cross marked "WELL" sits in the middle of the Sho'rko'l salt flats, where there has never been water in living memory. There is no expedition stamp.

This is not a survey. This is a decoy — drawn in a hurry, by someone who expected the briefcase to be searched.
r.c2.talk: Rudin answers every question with a question. Where do you keep the passengers' luggage tags? Did the professor have visitors before he… vanished? Is the baggage car at the back usually locked? "We are all servants of the common good, conductor. Some of us simply see further down the line." When you leave, you feel his eyes on the back of your neck like a draught.
r.c2_search.copy: You copy the telegram in your best handwriting, check every word twice, and lay the folder back under the pillow exactly as it was — the corner touching the seam. Even the dust looks undisturbed.
r.c2_search.pocket: You fold the telegram into your tunic and leave. It takes seconds. But a man like Rudin will notice an empty space in his folder the moment he sits down — and he will know whose hands are the only ones that have keys to every door.
r.c4.photo:
This time, when her hand goes to the photograph, she does not push it back. She gives it to you. A little girl on the shoulders of a bearded young man, mountains behind them; on the back, in faded ink: "Lola and Papa, Chimgan, 1961."

"He left when I was six," Lola says. "Mother never forgave him; I never asked him why. I found out he'd be on this train and I bought the ticket next to his. Three hundred kilometres, and I haven't said a word to him." She takes the photograph back. "And now he's gone."
r.c4.photo_no: Lola smiles thinly and changes the subject each time it comes near the photograph. "You have a carriage to run," she says at last, kindly but firmly. She needs to trust you more than she does.
r.c4.talk: You talk about the medical institute, about exams, about the hostel where the hot water runs for an hour on Thursdays. Lola answers politely, like a patient describing someone else's symptoms. Every so often her hand goes to the textbook, to the corner of the photograph sticking out of it, and pushes it back in. She is not ready to trust you with whatever that is.
r.c5.talk: Gena talks. About the 'Swallow' with its finest stitch in the republic, about his wife in Kogon who will kill him, about his debts — "cards, brother, the curse of my life" — and about "a generous friend" who has "lately taken an interest in my welfare". When you ask which friend, he laughs, slaps your knee and tries to sell you a spare bobbin. He will not say more for the asking.
r.c6.hen_no: Halima-buvi pulls the basket closer with her foot. "Malika doesn't like strangers, child. Neither do I, when it comes to my basket." She smiles, but the subject is closed. Perhaps if she knew you better — or if you had been kinder to her at the start of the night.
r.c6.talk:
She pours you tea from her own flask and talks in proverbs. "A guest is from God, but a thief is from the neighbour." Then she leans closer. "At half past ten I was awake — the drops hadn't taken me yet. The tall professor walked past my door towards the back of the train. In his socks, child, with his shoes in his hand, soft as a cat. And before that, the grey one went along the corridor trying every door handle, one after another, like a man counting his money."

She strokes Malika's back. "She's been sitting heavy all night. Like on eggs. And she hasn't laid since summer."
r.corridor.wait: You lean your forehead against the cold glass and let the steppe go by: a lonely light, a sleeping village, a dry riverbed white under the stars. When you straighten up, it is {time}.
r.d_comp4.calm: You make her sit, put your own jacket round her shoulders and talk about nothing — the weather in Qumtepa, the chef's terrible coffee. Slowly her breathing evens out. "He's my… I'm his student," she says, and the pause before "student" is so long you could drive a train through it. She does not explain, and you do not ask. Not yet.
r.dining.chat:
Bahodir's coffee could wake the dead, and his tongue never sleeps. "Your professor? Funny thing. At twenty-five to eleven I unlocked the baggage car to fetch a melon crate. Left the door open a minute — a minute! — came back, locked it. And I swear the door felt heavier, as if the car had swallowed something."

He leans in. "And another thing. My niece works the telegraph at Oltinsoy. A wire came for the professor: 'Meet you Qumtepa platform 6:00 with photographer — D. Rahimova, Qumtepa Truth.' A newspaper woman! Our grey friend dines at half past eleven, by the way, regular as a clock, till quarter to one."

As you leave he pushes a heel of bread and a lump of cheese into your hands. "For whoever you're feeding. You look like someone who's feeding somebody."
r.dining.key: Bahodir weighs you with his eyes the way he weighs flour. Then he unhooks a key on a red tag and drops it into your palm. "For you, because you're a decent person. If anyone asks, you stole it."
r.dining.key_no: Bahodir laughs and wipes a glass. "My key? To my melons? I've known you for one cup of coffee, friend. Come back when I know you better." He means it kindly. He also means it.
r.duty_tickets.match: You take the pasteboard triangle from your pocket and, while Rudin is busy lighting a cigarette, hold it against his ticket. The tear matches like two halves of a broken plate: "…02". Whatever he says, the man in grey was in compartment 4 tonight, close enough to the window to lose a piece of himself there.
r.ev_chief_round.fine: "All quiet, Matvey-aka." He grunts, taps the samovar with a knuckle, and moves on to carriage 8. The door of compartment 2 closes softly behind him.
r.ev_chief_round.key: Matvey looks at you for a long moment, then unhooks a key from his belt. "You've done your work tonight; I'll trust you with this. Back on my hook by Saksovul. And not a word to the ministry."
r.ev_chief_round.key_no: "The key? To my baggage car? When the tea's late and the tickets aren't done?" Matvey snorts. "Do your job first, then come and ask me for favours." He walks on.
r.ev_chief_round.report: Matvey's face goes from pink to beetroot. "Missing? Nobody goes missing on my train." He writes it in his book and underlines it twice. Your voices carry; the open door of compartment 2 does not close.
r.ev_gena_cards.decline: "Duty, duty," Gena sighs, putting the cards away. "You'll never get rich, brother." For a moment he looks almost relieved.
r.ev_gena_cards.play:
He lets you win — clumsily, like a man who has been paid to. Ten roubles drift to your side of the table. While he shuffles, you watch his hands: the fifty-rouble notes he pays with are brand new, consecutive, from an envelope with a ministry frank. Every time you glance towards compartment 2, Gena talks louder.

Forty minutes gone. Somewhere, the chief is checking his watch.
r.ev_inspection.cold: Matvey opens the samovar tap. Lukewarm water dribbles into the tray. He says nothing at all, which is worse. Coal — the one thing he asked for. He makes a mark in his book.
r.ev_inspection.ok: The samovar is hot, the glasses are clean, and Matvey's eyebrows climb a centimetre in approval. "Hot tea at five in the morning. Whatever else happened tonight, carriage 7 kept its samovar." He makes a mark in his book — a good one, for once.
r.ev_lights.guard: You collide with someone in the doorway of compartment 4 — a man, a coat, a smell of cloves. He shoves you against the wall and is gone. When the lights come back, Lola is sitting up, white-faced, and the professor's briefcase is gone. "He didn't touch me," she says. "He only wanted the case." Let him have it. You know what was in it.
r.ev_lights.search:
You feel your way along the wall to compartment 2 — empty, its owner busy elsewhere in the dark. Your fingers find the leather folder under the pillow, then a telegram form. You read it by the glow of a match, cupped in your hand:

TO V RUDIN TRAIN 17 CAR 7 STOP SAKSOVUL 0400 THREE MEN AND CAR READY STOP BRING GEOLOGIST WITH PAPERS STOP NO FUSS STOP K

You put everything back and are in the corridor when the lights return. Compartment 4's briefcase, you learn later, has vanished.
r.ev_lights.stay: You light a candle in compartment 6 and sit with Halima-buvi while Malika calms down. "In the dark, the honest man stays where he is," the old woman says, "and the thief goes walking." When the lights return, the professor's briefcase has vanished from compartment 4.
r.ev_rudin_attack.shout: "Gena!" The compartment door bangs and Gena Sorokin comes barrelling down the corridor in his vest, a sample case swinging like a club. "Brother! Is this man bothering you?" Rudin takes one look at the two of you, pulls the outer door shut, and walks away, straightening his cuffs. Gena is trembling. So are you.
r.ev_rudin_chat.dumb: You talk about the samovar, the linen count and the price of coal until his eyes glaze over. "Yes, yes," he says at last, and the banknote vanishes. "A simple man. How restful." He does not quite believe you. But he believes you a little more than before.
r.ev_rudin_chat.gift: The banknote is crisp and warm from his hand. "For keeping things tidy," Rudin says. "Tidy carriages, tidy minds." He pats your shoulder like a man patting a horse he has just bought. You feel lighter by twenty roubles' worth of something you cannot name.
r.ev_rudin_chat.push: Rudin taps ash into the dark gap of the gangway. "Water, conductor. I serve water. Somebody has to own it — the state, the people, who knows. The water itself doesn't care. It belongs to whoever can afford the pipes." He pockets the banknote. "You ask too many questions for a man who pours tea."
r.ev_rudin_threat.defy: "I'm a conductor, not a coat rack." For a moment something flickers in Rudin's face — surprise, almost respect — and then it's gone. "Pity," he says, and opens the door for you, politely, the way one opens the door of a cell.
r.ev_rudin_threat.promise: "Of course, comrade." The words taste of rust. Rudin nods, satisfied, and lets you go. Whether you meant it is between you and the night.
r.p_chief.ask: Matvey's moustache twitches. "The telegram came from the depot director himself. 'Assist Comrade Rudin in every way.' I don't ask questions of telegrams, and neither do you." He goes, but the question goes with him; you see it on his back.
r.p_professor.ask_baggage: "My samples travel there. Rocks dislike company." He smiles, but his eyes go to the door, to the corridor, to the door again. "Rocks keep secrets better than people, you know. That is why I like them."
r.rear.coal: You fill the scuttle and feed the samovar until it purrs. As you sweep the spilled coal back towards the bin, you notice footprints in the black dust — not boots, not shoes: stockinged feet, with no heel marks. They lead from the corridor door straight to the baggage car, and none of them come back.
r.rear.listen: Over the roar of the wheels you hear it: a small dry cough, high-pitched, from up near the ventilation hatch. Then a rustle, and a whisper not meant for you: "…if only there was bread…" When you call out, there is a scramble and then nothing at all. Whoever it is will not come out to an empty-handed stranger.
r.sherzod.thank: Sherzod shrugs, as if promises are something adults say, and climbs back into the hatch with the rest of the cheese. "I'll tell the militia too, if you want," his voice says out of the dark. "I'm not scared of militia. I'm scared of the grey one."
r.staff.orders: Among the usual notices — samovar hours, the linen count — there is a fresh carbon copy: "By request of the Ministry, render every assistance to Comrade V. Rudin, who will ALIGHT AT SAKSOVUL with a travelling companion." Saksovul. But Rudin told everyone he was going to Qumtepa. And he was travelling alone.
r.staff.sleep: You only mean to close your eyes. When you open them, your cheek is stuck to the ledger, the samovar has gone cold, and somebody — you can guess who — has been knocking on your door and then gone to tell the chief about it. It is {time}.
r.window:
The window is lowered only a hand's width — no grown man went through that gap. The brass latch is scratched, and there is grey graphite in the scratches: it was pushed up from inside with a pencil. The dust on the outer frame is undisturbed.

On the floor beneath the window lies a little triangle of pasteboard: the torn corner of a ticket, with half a printed number — "…02". Tickets are numbered by compartment on this line. You slip it into your pocket.
